analysis.one_liner: Designates millions of acres of Northern Rockies public land as wilderness and bans logging, mining, and new roads there.
analysis.headline: A public-lands bill with 111 backers in the House — 110 cosponsors plus its sponsor — never received a committee vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have protected the remaining roadless wild lands of Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Oregon, and Washington by adding about 13 million acres of national forest to the National Wilderness Preservation System, linking major ecosystems with biological corridors, creating a new Hells Canyon national preserve, and designating wild and scenic rivers. Once land is designated wilderness, logging, mining, oil and gas drilling, and new road construction are prohibited on it. The bill also created a restoration corps to repair damaged lands and guaranteed Native American access for traditional and religious uses.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who use and value public lands: hikers, hunters, anglers, and future visitors get permanent protection for wilderness, rivers, and wildlife habitat in the Northern Rockies. Downstream communities gain protection for watersheds that feed major river systems. Taxpayers stop funding timber sales and development on lands the bill itself found to be worth more left intact than harvested. Native American tribes gain guaranteed access to sacred areas, including a Blackfeet wilderness carved out with treaty rights recognized. A new Wildland Recovery Corps would create restoration jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who uses or values public lands

how_it_helps.text: Adds roughly 13 million acres of national forest land across Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Oregon, and Washington to the National Wilderness Preservation System, where timber harvest, mining, and new roads are prohibited.

Designates about 4.9 million acres of biological connecting corridors as wilderness and places another 2.5 million acres under special management barring even-aged logging, mining, oil and gas development, and new road construction.
Creates the Hells Canyon/Chief Joseph National Preserve, a new National Park System unit of about 1.4 million acres, and designates segments of Idaho rivers as wild and scenic rivers.

Guarantees Native Americans nonexclusive access to protected areas for traditional cultural and religious purposes, and designates a Blackfeet Wilderness that recognizes Blackfeet treaty rights in the Badger-Two Medicine area.

The bill's own findings state that the economic value of these undeveloped areas left in their natural state exceeds any return to the Treasury from timber harvest, meaning continued development would use tax dollars to fund permanent losses of wilderness, water quality, and habitat.
Establishes a National Wildland Recovery Corps within the Forest Service to restore lands damaged by logging and other development.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies lose access to roadless national forest available for harvest; mining and oil and gas companies lose access to lands withdrawn under the mining and mineral leasing laws. Grazing permittees in the new Hells Canyon preserve face buyouts of active allotments and closure of vacant ones. Motorized recreation users lose areas of access. Rural mountain-west communities that depend on extractive jobs and county revenue share would bear the local economic adjustment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests

drawbacks.text: Designating this much land as wilderness reduces logging, mining, and grazing activity in a region where some rural communities and county budgets depend on extractive industries and the shared revenue they generate, and the bill offers restoration work but no explicit transition aid for displaced workers.
The bill restricts motorized recreation and road access across vast areas, which off-road vehicle users and some residents of nearby communities view as closing off lands they currently use.

Top-down federal designation of this scale overrides state and local land-use preferences in the affected states; the bill's sponsors were largely from outside the region, and the designations would take management authority away from the local forest planning process.

Reserving federal water rights for each wilderness area with an enactment-date priority could complicate western water adjudications that determine how scarce water is allocated among farms, cities, and other users.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is permanent and enormous in scale, covering the largest remaining intact wild ecosystems in the lower 48 states, and the bill's design tries to soften the costs: highways and existing roads are expressly exempted, private landowners cannot be compelled to participate, and grazing buyouts are voluntary purchases from permittees. The real costs fall on extractive industries and the rural communities tied to them, and the bill provides no clear economic bridge for those places. Weighing permanent protection of habitat and headwaters against continued subsidized logging and mining on public land, the benefit side is much larger; the honest weakness is the absence of transition help for timber-dependent towns.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Resources Committee and then to two of its subcommittees the week after introduction, and it sat there without a hearing or a vote until the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 2, 1999 and referred to the House Committee on Resources.

Eight days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on National Parks and Public Lands and the Subcommittee on Forests and Forest Health, with executive comment requested from the Interior and Agriculture Departments.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a subcommittee or full committee vote and never reached the House floor before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
Support was broad on paper: 110 House members cosponsored, including 98 Democrats, 11 Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests are better off because the bill died: the roadless lands it would have withdrawn from development remain open to those uses, and the bill's own findings indicate those activities were often financed at a loss to taxpayers. The 111 members who backed it gained nothing; the public gained no new wilderness.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Extractive industries kept access to public lands

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Northern Rockies Ecosystem Protection Act and recruited the original 20 cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.role: Independent Representative (I-VT), the House's sole Independent member at the time

against.name: Rep. Don Young
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled a hearing or committee vote on it, leaving it in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines — 98 Democrats, 11 Republicans, and 1 Independent cosponsored — but the committee that kept the bill from a vote was run by the majority Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would bar timber harvest on roughly 13 million acres of roadless national forest and prohibit even-aged logging in corridor areas. Its findings state these lands yield less treasury revenue than they are worth undeveloped, meaning public logging there has been running partly at taxpayer expense.

industries.industry: Mining and oil and gas industry
industries.note: The bill withdraws designated wilderness, corridors, and study areas from entry under the mining laws and from geothermal and mineral leasing, and bans new exploration and development in special corridor management areas. Industry lost the option to develop millions of acres of federal land.

In the proposed Hells Canyon preserve, vacant allotments would be closed and active allotments purchased from willing permittees — compensation for some, loss of a subsidized grazing livelihood for others. The bill is silent on buying out allotments elsewhere.

industries.industry: Motorized recreation and off-road vehicle users
industries.note: Wilderness designation and corridor rules barring road construction would close large areas to motorized use and new road access. The bill exempts dozens of named existing highways and roads, but new motorized access is shut off.
Permanent wilderness, wild and scenic rivers, and a new national preserve protect the scenery, fisheries, and hunting and fishing habitat that draw visitors to the Northern Rockies.
